claim: Rosebury holds that Tolkien opens passages in plain modern language and modulates into a higher register only where the narrative touches ancient or magical history.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury 2003)
quote: modulating into a higher register to deal with echoes

verdict.trueWording: modulating into a higher register to deal with the echoes
verdict.note: Substance confirmed: 'Tolkien begins this in plain language, modulating into a higher register to deal with the echoes of ancient and magical history,' attributed to Rosebury. NOT verbatim: the claim's quote drops the definite article ('with echoes' vs 'with the echoes'). Also note the page says 'plain language', not 'plain modern language', and asserts no 'only where' exclusivity.

claim: Turner argues Tolkien assigns discrete linguistic registers to different peoples: simple and modern for Hobbits, more archaic for Dwarves, Elves and the Rohirrim.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Turner 2020/2022)
quote: discrete linguistic registers for different characters, peoples

verdict.trueWording: discrete linguistic registers for different characters, peoples, and cultures
verdict.note: Exact string present in the rendered article: 'Turner states that The Lord of the Rings makes use of several styles of prose, with discrete linguistic registers for different characters, peoples, and cultures.' The Hobbit/Dwarf/Elf/Rohirrim contrast follows in the same sentence group. Caveat: the page cites this to Turner 2013 (pp. 545-546), not Turner 2020/2022 as the claim's source line states; Turner 2020 is cited elsewhere for a different point.

claim: Turner's Companion chapter abstract states that stylistic features become a means of distinguishing characters and their different cultural and ethical outlooks, with local and temporal colour supplied by intertextual references to older literatures.
source: Turner 2022, 'Style and Intertextual Echoes', A Companion to J. R. R. Tolkien (abstract via OpenAlex)

verdict.trueWording: are on their way to becoming a means of distinguishing
verdict.note: OpenAlex record confirms Allan Turner, 'Style and Intertextual Echoes', 2022, correct DOI. Abstract (reconstructed from the inverted index) reads 'Stylistic features are on their way to becoming a means of distinguishing between different characters and different cultural and ethical outlooks' and 'Tolkien was able to achieve local and temporal color by including a high proportion of intertextual references to older literatures.' The claim drops the abstract's hedge, asserting features 'become' rather than 'are on their way to becoming'.

claim: Shippey holds that the Hobbits' modern idiom lets them mediate between the modern reader and the heroic, archaic world of the epic.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Shippey 2005)

verdict.trueWording: Hobbits serve as mediators between the modern world and fantasy realm
verdict.note: Page: 'Shippey explains that the Hobbits serve as mediators between the ordinary modern world and the heroic and archaic fantasy realm, making The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings readily accessible,' cited to Shippey 2005 p. 259 — matching the claim's stated source. Wording differs: 'ordinary modern world' not 'modern reader', and 'fantasy realm' not 'world of the epic'. No quote was offered, so verbatim status is not at issue.

claim: Shippey reads 'The Council of Elrond', roughly fifteen thousand words consisting entirely of talk, as a tour de force in which each of many speakers is given a distinct idiom.
source: 'An Analysis of Scholarship on Tolkien: The Council of Elrond' (student synthesis of Shippey)

verdict.trueWording: Shippey argues Tolkien does an extraordinary job
verdict.note: Page supports the length and the all-talk character: readers 'may dismiss it as a waste of fifteen thousand words because there is little to no action, other than people conversing back and forth,' and Shippey credits Tolkien's 'integration of cultural variation' (Shippey 68-69), with distinct voices demonstrated for Elrond, Gloin, Boromir and Aragorn. But 'tour de force' appears nowhere on the page (zero occurrences); the essay's phrase is 'does an extraordinary job'. That framing is the claim's own.

claim: Shippey states that Elrond's archaism is consistent and achieved not just by vocabulary but also by grammar.
source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'To Make a Soul' (quoting Shippey)
quote: achieved not just by vocabulary...but also by grammar

verdict.trueWording: achieved not just by vocabulary ... but also by grammar
verdict.note: The page quotes Shippey directly: '...Elrond's archaism is consistent, achieved not just by vocabulary (the first resort of the amateur medievalist), but also by grammar' (p. 76). Both fragments on either side of the claim's ellipsis appear word for word, and the ellipsis honestly marks the elided parenthetical. Attribution to Shippey and the consistency point both check out.

claim: In Shippey's reading Boromir uses inverted constructions close to Elrond's idiom, while Aragorn in the same scene speaks colloquially.
source: 'An Analysis of Scholarship on Tolkien: The Council of Elrond' (synthesis of Shippey)
quote: inverted constructions

verdict.trueWording: inverted constructions
verdict.note: Exact match in context: 'Boromir is most closely associated with Elrondian, utilizing "inverted constructions," whereas Aragorn is more colloquial (72-73).' Both halves of the claim — Boromir's proximity to Elrond's idiom and Aragorn's colloquialism in the same Council scene — are directly supported.

claim: Aragorn's speech register shifts with situation, colloquial among hobbits and formal in high settings, a high/low alternation the essay likens to Auerbach's sermo humilis.
source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'Sublimis and Humilis; Aragorn and Strider'
quote: His manner of speech changes directly with the situation

verdict.trueWording: His manner of speech changes directly with the situation
verdict.note: Exact sentence present, continuing '...and represents the dual nature of Aragorn and Strider.' The colloquial-among-hobbits and formal-in-high-settings halves are both borne out ('Around the hobbits... can talk very colloquially'; 'when presented with a formal situation, Aragorn can quickly switch'). Minor caveat: the compound term 'sermo humilis' does not appear; the essay quotes Auerbach's Mimesis as 'the low style was sermo remissus or humilis' against 'sermo gravis or sublimis', and explicitly parallels Aragorn's high/low contrast to it.

claim: Saruman's duplicity is conveyed through politically minded, abstract modern speech.
source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'To Make a Soul'
quote: politically minded, abstract manners of speech

verdict.trueWording: politically minded, abstract manners of speech
verdict.note: Exact match: 'Saruman's duplicity can be felt through his politically minded, abstract manners of speech.' Caveat on the claim's paraphrase and its 'modern idiom' feature label: the page does not describe Saruman's speech as modern — that adjective is the claim's addition, and this page's modernity discussion attaches to other characters.

claim: Tolkien imagined the Rohirrim speaking the Common Speech more slowly and deliberately because it was their second language.
source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'To Make a Soul' (citing Tolkien's letter to Tiller)
quote: much slower and more deliberate

verdict.trueWording: much slower and more deliberate
verdict.note: Exact match: 'Tolkien even went to far as to consider the tone and cadence with which the Rohirrim would speak C.S.; it being their second language, he imagined it would be much slower and more deliberate.' Both the second-language reason and the Common Speech referent are explicit. Caveat: this sentence is not itself tied to the Tiller letter on the page — the letter to Terrence Tiller is cited two sentences later for a different quotation (on 'linguistic differentiation... in diction, idiom', p. 254).

claim: Rosebury identifies three types of Orc dialogue keyed to rank; Grishnákh speaks like a melodrama villain while Gorbag uses grumbling twentieth-century bureaucratic speech.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury 2003)
quote: three types of Orc-dialogue for different ranks

verdict.trueWording: three types of Orc-dialogue for different ranks
verdict.note: Exact string present, attributed to Rosebury 2003 pp. 81-83: 'Tolkien had in fact created at least three types of Orc-dialogue for different ranks and tribes.' Grishnakh as melodrama villain is also Rosebury ('like a melodrama villain, or a public-school bully'). Two caveats: the page says 'at least three', and the twentieth-century bureaucratic reading of Gorbag belongs to Vaninskaya ('minor officials in a murderous bureaucracy'), not Rosebury — the lead only calls Gorbag's speech 'grumbling modern speech'. The claim folds two scholars into one.

claim: Vaninskaya reads the Orcs' speech as the twentieth-century idiom of soldiers, functionaries and minor officials.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Vaninskaya 2020)

verdict.trueWording: the speech of the twentieth century, whether as soldiers, functionaries
verdict.note: Page: 'Anna Vaninskaya writes that the most modern idiom in The Lord of the Rings is used by the Orcs... Tolkien gives them the speech of the twentieth century, whether as soldiers, functionaries in party or government, or "minor officials in a murderous bureaucracy"' (Vaninskaya 2020, p. 363) — matching the claim's stated source. All three of the claim's categories are present; no quote was offered.

claim: Rosebury describes Gollum's extraordinary idiolect of obsessive repetition and infantile whining; the translation literature adds ungrammatical syntax, 'pocketses' plurals and I/we confusion.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury 2003)
quote: obsessive repetition, infantile whining

verdict.trueWording: its obsessive repetition, its infantile whining, its minimal syntax
verdict.note: Rosebury half supported: Gollum's 'extraordinary idiolect' is Tolkien's 'most memorable success' of voice, 'with its obsessive repetition, its infantile whining, its minimal syntax and its unstable sense of being one or two people' (Rosebury 2003, pp. 81-83). NOT verbatim: the claim's quote drops the possessive 'its' before 'infantile whining'. The second half fails on this source — 'pocketses' and 'ungrammatical' appear nowhere on the page (zero occurrences), and no translation literature is discussed; the nearest support is 'minimal syntax' and the 'unstable sense of being one or two people' for the I/we confusion.

claim: Kullmann and Siepmann find all eight members of the Fellowship clearly distinguished by their style of speech.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Kullmann & Siepmann 2021)
quote: eight members clearly distinguished by style of speech

verdict.trueWording: eight members are clearly distinguished by their style of speech
verdict.note: Page (Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, pp.259-296) supports the substance, but the supplied quote is a compression, not contiguous text. Full sentence: 'the eight members of the Fellowship of the Ring (barring Boromir, who dies early in the narrative) are clearly distinguished by their style of speech.' Note the claim's 'all eight members of the Fellowship' drops the Boromir carve-out: the Fellowship has nine members, and the eight are the nine minus Boromir, so 'all' is inexact. A table on the page details each of the eight.

claim: Shippey holds that Tolkien understood archaism technically enough to switch it on and off at will, as he could modern colloquialism, and that this linguistic control is among his least appreciated abilities.
source: Salka Wind blog, 'Language, Thought, and Worldviews in Tolkien's Writing' (quoting Shippey)
quote: could switch it on and off at will

verdict.trueWording: could switch it on and off at will
verdict.note: Both halves confirmed, from two separate Shippey quotations on the page. Quote verbatim (pg 70): 'they have failed to realize that he understood archaism far more technically than they ever could, and could switch it on and off at will, as he could modern colloquialism.' The 'least appreciated' clause is also verbatim, from a second quote (pg 76): 'Tolkien's linguistic control (a professional skill for him) is one of his least appreciated abilities.' A partial read of the page would have wrongly scored that clause unsupported.

claim: In Letter 171 Tolkien rejects the 'tushery' charge, arguing real archaic English is terser than modern English, which is looser and full of little empty words.
source: Salka Wind blog (quoting Tolkien, Letter 171)
quote: looser, more full of little 'empty' words

verdict.trueWording: looser, more full of little 'empty' words
verdict.note: Verbatim on page: 'modern English is regrettably looser, more full of little empty words' (page uses curly apostrophes around 'empty'; wording otherwise identical). 'Terser' is confirmed too: 'Archaic English provides word orders that are terser.' Tushery context confirmed: the student called the chapter tushery, and Tolkien's reply calls modern-English phrasing 'far more bogus than the actual archaic English'. Caveat: this is the blogger's indirect report of Letter 171, not a directly quoted Tolkien passage.

claim: Tolkien claims archaic English offers word orders that are terser, more vivid and sometimes nobler, and that a king speaking modern English would not have had those thoughts.
source: Salka Wind blog (quoting Tolkien, Letter 171)
quote: terser, more vivid, and sometimes nobler

verdict.trueWording: terser, more vivid, and sometimes nobler
verdict.note: Quote verbatim: 'Archaic English provides word orders that are terser, more vivid, and sometimes nobler than modern English.' Second half also confirmed on page: 'But, Tolkien states, a King who spoke in that modern fashion would not have had those thoughts!' — said of Théoden in 'The King of the Golden Hall'.

claim: Walker holds that the Riders of Rohan are given Anglo-Saxon syntactic patterns and a diction that is stirring, alliteratively stately and stern.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Walker 2009)
quote: stirring, alliteratively stately

verdict.trueWording: stirring, alliteratively stately, [and] stern
verdict.note: Verbatim, both quoted elements, cited to Walker 2009 p.143: 'Tolkien goes furthest with the Riders of Rohan, giving them "Anglo-Saxon syntactic patterns" and diction which is "stirring, alliteratively stately, [and] stern".' The 'and' is bracketed in the source as an editorial insertion.

claim: The Rohirrim's speech carries actual Old English words and phrases such as éored, dwimmerlaik and mearas, and the Dwarves' speech is archaic, blunt and proverbial.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style'

verdict.trueWording: words rescued from total obscurity: éored, dwimmerlaik, mearas
verdict.note: Rohirrim half fully confirmed: Tolkien gives Rohan speakers words 'rescued from total obscurity' like éored (OE 'a troop of cavalry'), dwimmerlaik, and mearas, plus Éomer's phrase directly in Old English, 'Westu Théoden hál!'. The Dwarves half is a loose synthesis, not a source statement: the page says Tolkien makes 'the other Council members' (Elrond, an Elf, as well as the Dwarf Glóin) speak in an 'archaic, blunt, clearsighted' way — not the Dwarves specifically — and 'proverbial' has been substituted for 'clearsighted'. Proverbs are attributed to Gimli and Legolas in the speech table, not to Dwarves as a people.

claim: Wilton catalogues Old English embedded in the prose: 'Westu Théoden hál', dwimmerlaik (dweomer + -lác), the hobbit words mathom and smial (smygel), and names like Orthanc and Dwarrowdelf.
source: Wordorigins.org, 'Old English in LoTR' (David Wilton)

verdict.trueWording: dweomer (illusion) + -lác; smial from Old English smygel
verdict.note: No quotation was supplied, so verbatim does not apply, but every catalogued item checks out on David Wilton's page (wordorigins.org, dated 1 December 2002; Wilton confirmed as the site's author). Confirmed: 'Westu Théoden hál' as Éomer's greeting; dwimmerlaik from dweomer (illusion, phantasm) + -lác (suffix of action or condition), via Middle English demerlayk; mathom and smial as hobbit words, smial based on OE smygel (burrow); Orthanc (OE 'contrivance, skill, intelligence'); Dwarrowdelf from dweorh + gedelf. Also present: mearas, éoreds, Théoden, Éomer, Éowyn.

claim: Turner's example of fronting, placing the object before the verb, is 'Weapons they have laid at your doors', a construction he notes cannot be reproduced in French and is unmarked in German.
source: Wikipedia, 'Translating The Lord of the Rings' (citing Turner)
quote: Weapons they have laid at your doors

verdict.trueWording: Weapons they have laid at your doors
verdict.note: Fully verbatim and every element confirmed: 'Allan Turner gives the example of fronting, where Tolkien puts the object at the start of a sentence rather than after the verb: "Weapons they have laid at your doors". Turner points out that this cannot be done in French, while in German it remains a common construction and doesn't give an archaic effect.' The claim's 'unmarked in German' correctly renders the last point. Sourced to Smith 2006 citing Turner 2005.

feature: Old English to Modern English mapping
claim: Shippey explains that Tolkien rendered Rohirric as Old English so that its relation to Westron mirrors Old English's relation to Modern English.
source: Wikipedia, 'Translating The Lord of the Rings' (citing Shippey)

verdict.trueWording: mapping of Old English to Modern English represents Rohirric to Westron
verdict.note: Substance is on the page, but the attribution to Shippey is imprecise. The exact mapping sentence appears in a gallery IMAGE CAPTION cited to Tolkien's own essay 'The Rivers and Beacon-hills of Gondor' (Vinyar Tengwar 42), not to Shippey. Shippey (2005, pp.131-133) is cited in the adjacent paragraph for the related points: that Tolkien chose Old English for names and words of the Rohirrim, and that 'the relation of such names to English... is intended to reflect the relation of the purported original names to Westron.'

claim: Siepmann's corpus study finds the reader's impression of archaicity has three lexical causes: overuse of nineteenth-century fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense coinages, unusual grammar and rare or obsolescent words.
source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation' (CL2017, Birmingham)
quote: three simple lexical causes

verdict.trueWording: three simple lexical causes
verdict.note: Quote verbatim and all three causes match exactly: 'the impression of archaicity which any reader will experience on reading Lord of the Rings is partly due to three simple lexical causes: the overuse of words borrowed from nineteenth-century fiction, the avoidance of words associated with the modern world, and the comparatively dense use of new coinages, unusual grammatical patterns, rare or obsolescent words.' One hedge to preserve: the paper says 'partly due to', where the claim says the impression 'has' three causes.

claim: Key words shared with a 30-million-word nineteenth-century fiction corpus cluster in landscape, position/direction, warfare, and descriptive verbs and adjectives, many obsolescent when Tolkien wrote.
source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
quote: whither, thither, thence, whence, upwards, yonder, afar

verdict.trueWording: whither, thither, thence, whence, upwards, yonder, afar
verdict.note: Quoted word run appears verbatim and in that order. The four lexical sets match the claim exactly: '(1) landscape description; (2) position or direction; (3) warfare and the struggle between good and evil; (4) other descriptive verbs and adjectives.' Corpus size confirmed twice: 'The 19th century corpus was about 30 million words in size' and 'a 30-million word corpus of nineteenth-century novels'. Obsolescence confirmed: 'so many of the keywords used to describe its settings were obsolete or obsolescent at the time of writing.'

claim: Tolkien borrows words such as valour, valiant and corslet from his own Beowulf translation and stretches them to wider uses than Old or Middle English allowed.
source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
quote: Branched lightning smote down upon the eastward hills

verdict.trueWording: Branched lightning smote down upon the eastward hills
verdict.note: Verbatim, and the whole sentence supports the claim: 'Tolkien borrows a host of words from his translation of Beowulf (e.g. valour, valiant, corslet), stretching them creatively to cover a wider range of uses than was possible in Old or Middle English (e.g. Branched lightning smote down upon the eastward hills.)' All three sample words confirmed.

claim: Modern core-vocabulary key words (they, big, wake, smoke) are used in nineteenth-century grammatical patterns, e.g. 'smoke' with an indefinite article.
source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
quote: a black smoke swirled in the air

verdict.trueWording: a black smoke swirled in the air
verdict.note: Verbatim: 'One example among many is smoke, which is commonly preceded by the indefinite article in Lord of the Rings (e.g. ... a black smoke swirled in the air.), a use that is notably infrequent in modern fiction.' Core-vocabulary list confirmed: 'they, big, wake, wall, unfriendly, tired or smoke.' Minor: the paper says these are used 'in nineteenth-century patterns'; the claim's added word 'grammatical' is fair given the indefinite-article example, but is not the paper's wording there.

claim: Tolkien follows modernist tendencies in his heavy use of manner-laden descriptive verbs such as clutch, cower, flicker, gleam, glint, loom, plod and stride.
source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
quote: abundant use of descriptive verbs

verdict.trueWording: abundant use of descriptive verbs
verdict.note: Quote verbatim: 'One area in which Tolkien tends to follow modernist tendencies is his abundant use of descriptive verbs.' The claim's 'manner-laden' correctly renders the paper's definition: verbs containing 'an additional semantic feature that assumes the function of a manner adverb' (citing Snell-Hornby 1983). All eight verbs cited in the claim — clutch, cower, flicker, gleam, glint, loom, plod, stride — appear in the paper's key-verb list.

claim: Words key only to Tolkien (fastness, sheath, lore-masters, gaffer, wolf-riders, yesteryear, yuledays, along, among, outwards) are rare rather than archaic but together create an atmosphere of medievalism.
source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
quote: atmosphere of medievalism or otherworldliness

verdict.trueWording: work together to create an atmosphere of medievalism or otherworldliness
verdict.note: Siepmann p.3 (PDF p.2-3): the LOTR-exclusive key-word lists contain all ten cited items (fastness, sheath / lore-masters, gaffer, wolf-riders / yesteryear, yuledays / along, among, outwards), followed by 'most of these words are comparatively rare in present-day English and, although not archaic, work together to create an atmosphere of medievalism or otherworldliness.' Quote exact; 'rare rather than archaic' exact in substance.

claim: Tolkien prefers the most homely collocations but uses everyday adjectives like 'great' with peril, deeds, trees, halls, shadow and smoke at densities beyond nineteenth-century fiction.
source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
quote: marked preference for the most homely collocations

verdict.trueWording: Tolkien shows a marked preference for the most homely collocations available
verdict.note: Siepmann p.3. Quote exact. 'Great' is listed with peril, deed (claim says 'deeds'), force, power, strength; trees, stones, halls, horns, gates; clouds, storms, shadow, wind, smoke — and 'These collocations are derived from 19th century fiction, where they occur much less frequently, though', which supports the density point.

claim: Key semantic domains for entire/maximum, loud, hot, and long/tall/wide support the hypothesis that Tolkien tends toward hyperbole, while dense plant vocabulary (elm-tree, alder, rowan, hemlock) supplies circumstantial realism.
source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
quote: Tolkien tends to resort to hyperbole

verdict.trueWording: lending additional weight to the hypothesis that Tolkien tends to resort to hyperbole
verdict.note: Quote exact (Siepmann p.3). CAVEAT on the second half: the source names FIVE domains ('speed:fast (slow)', 'entire/maximum', 'sound:loud', 'temperature:hot/on fire', 'long, tall and wide') — the claim silently drops speed. More importantly, the source does NOT attribute circumstantial realism to the plant vocabulary; it assigns that to 'general appearance and physical properties', 'geographical terms', 'farming and horticulture' and 'fixing and mending', and treats 'plants' separately as a domain key-word analysis misses. That linkage is the claimant's extrapolation. ('alder' appears as 'alder-tree'.)

claim: Siepmann concludes the prose deploys several centuries of linguistic development, putting old words to new uses and vice versa, making Tolkien a linguistic postmodernist.
source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
quote: he is a linguistic postmodernist

verdict.trueWording: employs several centuries' worth of linguistic developments... he is a linguistic postmodernist
verdict.note: Siepmann's closing paragraph, p.3, verbatim: 'Tolkien's prose effectively employs several centuries' worth of linguistic developments, putting old words to new uses and vice versa. In a much less obvious sense than in the case of James Joyce or Virginia Woolf, he is a linguistic postmodernist.' The claim drops the qualifier 'in a much less obvious sense than... Joyce or Woolf'.

claim: Lee reports Kullmann and Siepmann's finding that LOTR shares about twice as many key words with nineteenth-century fiction as with late twentieth-century fiction.
source: Lee 2022, 'Where many paths and errands meet: A Close Reading of The Lord of the Rings' (ORA PDF)
quote: around twice as many key words with nineteenth-century fiction

verdict.trueWording: around twice as many key words with nineteenth-century fiction
verdict.note: Lee p.9: 'Kullmann and Siepmann note that The Lord of the Rings shares "around twice as many key words with nineteenth-century fiction as it does with late twentieth-century fiction" (2021, 53) which they conclude gives it a distinctly archaic feel.' Quote exact, attribution exact.

claim: In the Siege of Gondor passage Lee lists real English words fallen from use that feel archaic: hardiest, wreck, slain, foe, thrice, asunder, riven, steadfast, abyss, behold.
source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)

verdict.trueWording: actual English words that have fallen out of general use
verdict.note: No quote supplied, so verbatim is not assessable. Lee p.9: '...actual English words that have fallen out of general use and feel archaic – "hardiest", "wreck", "slain", "foe", "thrice", "asunder", "riven", "steadfast", "abyss", "behold!", "mantled", "recking".' All ten cited items are on the list in the cited order; the claim omits the final two ('mantled', 'recking') and prints 'behold' for the source's 'behold!'.

claim: Lee finds the most common syntactic device in the passage is fronting of the object, often to pick up something named in the previous sentence.
source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)

verdict.trueWording: The most common device is one of 'fronting' where the object is moved
verdict.note: Lee p.9: 'The most common device is one of "fronting" where the object is moved to the beginning, often referring to something just mentioned in a previous sentence (e.g. "Grond crawled on. Upon its housing no fire would catch").' Quote exact. Source says 'the most common device' within the syntax discussion; 'syntactic' is the claimant's word, consistent with context.

claim: Lee identifies delayed adjectives ('the orcs innumerable', 'a mouth unseen') and inversion with delayed subject as recurrent devices.
source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
quote: In rode the Lord of the Nazgûl

verdict.trueWording: the delay of adjectives... and inversion with the delay of the subject
verdict.note: Lee p.9: 'There is also the delay of adjectives – "the orcs innumerable", "a mouth unseen"; and inversion with the delay of the subject – "Over the hills of slain a hideous shape appeared", and "In rode the Lord of the Nazgûl".' Quote and both adjective examples exact.

claim: Lee argues inverted syntax combined with archaic lexis evokes older books including the Bible and produces delay and suspense.
source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
quote: the inverted syntax creates delay and suspense

verdict.trueWording: a sense of past (calling to mind older books, including the Bible)
verdict.note: Lee p.9: 'Combined with the language used this reinforces a sense of past (calling to mind older books, including the Bible) and the inverted syntax creates delay and suspense.' Quote exact; both halves of the claim (Bible/older books, delay and suspense) in one sentence.

claim: Manuscript evidence shows Tolkien revising sentences to add alliteration, replacing 'like thunder' with 'and rattled' after 'drums rolled'.
source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
quote: seeing the further opportunity for alliteration

verdict.trueWording: seeing the further opportunity for alliteration he then crossed through 'like thunder'
verdict.note: Lee pp.9-10: 'Similarly Tolkien expanded the phrase "The drums rolled" (in Di 17a) to "The drums rolled like thunder" (E 21a) but seeing the further opportunity for alliteration he then crossed through "like thunder" in E and replaced it with "and rattled".' Quote exact; the revision direction (replacing 'like thunder' with 'and rattled') is exact.

claim: Lee shows from typescripts that Tolkien deliberately condensed the climactic prose into short sentences piled one on another, matching Kullmann and Siepmann's 'short, stark sentences' of the epic mode.
source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
quote: Tolkien deliberately condensed the prose

verdict.trueWording: manuscript evidence shows that Tolkien deliberately condensed the prose
verdict.note: Lee p.10: 'In terms of space, short sentences come one on top of each other and manuscript evidence shows that Tolkien deliberately condensed the prose.' Quote exact. CAVEAT: the claim says 'from typescripts' — the source says MANUSCRIPT evidence, and its footnote 28 cites MS Di (17a); the typescripts E/F/G are adduced for the caesurae, not the condensation. The Kullmann and Siepmann attribution is right: fn.28 quotes their 'short, stark sentences' conveying a sense of 'epic' (2021, 115-116).

claim: Lee traces medieval-poetic devices of variation (magnifying a character by renaming) and repetition into the prose, e.g. the triple 'Horns, horns, horns' with identity withheld to the final sentence.
source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)

All four exceptions confirmed: 'Shippey's Road and Flieger's Splintered Light, do effectively discuss elements of Tolkien's style. Shippey's Author likewise addresses head-on the issues of archaism, diction, and shifting voice... Brian Rosebury also does a commendable job investigating Tolkien's style'; and separately 'Paul Edmund Thomas does an admirable job of looking at Tolkien's style in his investigation of some of Tolkien's narrators.'

claim: Stimpson (1969) charged that Tolkien shuns ordinary diction and wrenches syntax, inventing 'To an eyot he came' as an example.

verdict.trueWording: shun[s] ordinary diction, he also wrenches syntax
verdict.note: Verbatim including the bracketed [s]: 'Catharine R. Stimpson, a scholar of English, wrote in 1969 that Tolkien not only "shun[s] ordinary diction, he also wrenches syntax". She supported her argument by inventing what she asserted were Tolkienistic sentences such as "To an eyot he came."' The 1969 date and the invented-example framing both match.

claim: Rosebury answers Stimpson item by item, locating the three real uses of 'eyot' and arguing their syntax is unexceptional twentieth-century English that Hemingway could have written.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury)

verdict.trueWording: Ernest Hemingway could have written them
verdict.note: No quotation was supplied to check, so this is graded on substance, which the page fully supports. 'Brian Rosebury systematically replies to each item in Stimpson's attack, showing that Tolkien mostly uses plain modern English. He locates the three places where Tolkien uses "eyot", arguing that "island" could not in these instances be used instead without loss of meaning... All three, Rosebury writes, are unexceptional in 20th century syntax: "Ernest Hemingway could have written them".' Item-by-item reply, three uses, unexceptional 20th-century syntax, and the Hemingway comparison all confirmed.

claim: Rosebury shows Tolkien favouring plain descriptive phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off' over the more literary 'wear' and 'dismount', and rejects unsupported charges of archaising and wrenched syntax.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien: A Cultural Phenomenon'
quote: a certain sensuous precision, distinctive of Tolkien

verdict.trueWording: familiar phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off'
verdict.note: Substance confirmed, but the supplied quote is a decoy. The supporting passage: 'Allan Turner comments in the same work that Rosebury rejects the unsupported assertions of archaising and "wrenched syntax" by critics like Catharine Stimpson, and that Rosebury pointed out that Tolkien used a plain descriptive style, demonstrably favouring the "familiar phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off' .. to the slightly more literary 'wear' and 'dismount'".' The quoted phrase 'a certain sensuous precision, distinctive of Tolkien' DOES appear verbatim on the page, but in an unrelated passage several paragraphs earlier — Nancy-Lou Patterson in Mythlore liking Rosebury's characterisation of 'Tolkien's descriptive gifts'. It is not evidence for the phrasal-verb claim; the citation should be repointed to the Turner sentence.

claim: Rosebury reads the Witch-king passage as making effective use of inversion together with assonance and alliteration to produce a powerfully musical sentence.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury)
quote: powerfully musical sentence

verdict.trueWording: powerfully musical sentence
verdict.note: Verbatim, and the surrounding analysis matches on every element: Rosebury notes the shift heralded by 'But glad would he have been', 'with effective use of inversion'; then 'The passage ends with a powerfully musical sentence with assonances between "blade", "wield", "dealt" and so on; alliteration with "wield", "wound", "will"'. The passage is indeed the Witch-king one (Merry's blade, 'the sword of the Barrow-Downs').

claim: Turner characterises the base style as paratactic, sentences without subordinate clauses or causal conjunctions, with repeated 'and'.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Turner)

verdict.trueWording: sentences without subordinate clauses or causal conjunctions
verdict.note: No quotation was supplied, so graded on substance, which is fully supported. 'Allan Turner... demonstrated with examples that Tolkien's style is both generally simple, using parataxis – sentences without subordinate clauses or causal conjunctions – and varied'. The repeated 'and' is confirmed separately: 'Turner notes that the paratactic style here, with the repeated use of "and" in the manner of the New Testament, is "stylistically marked"'. Note the article pairs 'generally simple' with 'and varied' — the claim's 'base style' framing is fair but drops Turner's second half.

claim: Kullmann and Siepmann define the epic register in LOTR by archaic diction, parataxis, plentiful imagery and poetic description, and count 45 to 50 embedded stories told by 23 narrators.

quote: archaic diction, parataxis, plentiful imagery

verdict.trueWording: archaic diction, parataxis with clauses linked with 'and'
verdict.note: Substance fully confirmed; the quotation is not contiguous. The article reads 'The epic style is characterised by archaic diction, parataxis with clauses linked with "and", plentiful imagery, and a richly poetical use of descriptive words' — the claim's quote 'archaic diction, parataxis, plentiful imagery' elides 'with clauses linked with "and"', so it is not word for word. The counts are exact: 'There are some 45 to 50 stories embedded in the text of The Lord of the Rings, supposedly narrated by 23 of the novel's characters', cited to Kullmann and Siepmann 2021, pp. 193–226.

claim: Rosebury traces Tolkien's development from an early sustained archaism modelled on William Morris to the mature intimate paternal storytelling style of LOTR.

verdict.trueWording: a sustained archaism
verdict.note: Verbatim: 'His prose uses "a sustained archaism" that harked back to William Morris (Rosebury, 95).' The developmental arc matches too: the post attributes it to 'Brian Rosebury, in his chapter "Fiction and Poetry"', tracing 1914–1973, and concludes 'when Tolkien finally achieved the "intimate paternal story-telling" style in his composition of the LOTR, his poetry was no longer conventional pastiche and his prose no longer weighed down by impossibly heavy archaism (Rosebury, 117).'

claim: Le Guin (as summarised) credits the prose with a simple timelessness that avoids both thee/thou archaism and modern slang; Sperling adds that Elrond stays consistently archaic while Aragorn can be wholly colloquial.
source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'A Hobbit Book: The Simplicity of Style'
quote: simple timelessness

verdict.trueWording: simple timelessness
verdict.note: Verbatim: 'LeGuin calls his language "an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness."' Both avoidances confirmed in the next sentences: 'by not trying to force the reader into a world of "thee" and "thou"' and 'his avoidance of most modern slang keeps his writing timeless.' The Sperling half is also exact — the post is signed '--Micah Sperling' and reads: 'Elrond's syntax and choice of words could be accused of archaism, but it is consistently archaic... Aragorn, on the other hand, can speak in completely colloquial modern English with just a hint of formality in the background.'

claim: Le Guin counted stresses and finds Tolkien's prose runs at the normal narrative ratio of one stress per two to four syllables, rising toward poetry's one-in-two in intense passages.
source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (The Wave in the Mind, PDF)
quote: one stress every two to four syllables

verdict.trueWording: one stress every two to four syllables
verdict.note: Verbatim: 'Tolkien's prose runs to the normal narrative ratio of one stress every two to four syllables.' The counting is confirmed ('I got interested in the ratio of stresses to syllables in prose, and did some counting'), as is the rise in intense passages: 'In passages of intense action and feeling the ratio may get pretty close to 50 percent, like poetry.' Small precision note: Le Guin's baseline for poetry is 'one syllable out of every two or three', so 'poetry's one-in-two' matches the 50 percent figure rather than her general poetry ratio.

claim: Le Guin insists the prose remains irregular and cannot be scanned, the sole exception being Tom Bombadil, whose speech is verse printed as prose with an infectious beat picked up by Goldberry and Frodo.
source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
quote: it is irregular, it can't be scanned

verdict.trueWording: except for Tom, it is irregular, it can't be scanned
verdict.note: Verbatim, and the sole-exception framing is explicit: '...but still, except for Tom, it is irregular, it can't be scanned', reinforced by 'If there are other metric passages in the Trilogy, I've missed them.' The verse-printed-as-prose point is confirmed twice: 'once at least in the Trilogy he quietly slips from prose into verse without signalling it typographically' and 'Usually Tom's speech is printed without line breaks, so unwary or careless silent readers may miss the beat until they see it as verse.' The infectious beat too: 'it's an infectious beat; it echoes in Goldberry's speech, and Frodo picks it up.'

claim: Le Guin finds the speech of Elves and noble folk such as Aragorn has a dignified, stately gait without a regular stress-beat, and Théoden only occasionally drops into iambics.

I suspected King Theoden of iambics, but he only drops into them occasionally, as all measured English speech does.' Both halves of the claim confirmed.

claim: Le Guin identifies the rhythm shaping the whole narrative as the simplest possible, two beats of stress and release, a walking gait, a trochaic alternation contemporaries found simplistic.

The 'trochaic'/simplistic element is also confirmed on p.89: 'This "trochaic" alternation of stress and relief...' and 'To readers with such expectations, Tolkien's plodding stress/relief pattern seemed and seems simplistic, primitive.'

claim: Scanning 'Fog on the Barrow-downs', Le Guin found each of a set of polarities (darkness/daylight, resting/traveling, confusion/clarity, menace/ease, imprisonment/freedom, fear/courage) reversed three or four times in the chapter.

verdict.trueWording: a positive/negative binary pattern of alternation or reversal
verdict.note: Quote verbatim (p.89). All six named polarities are on her list: darkness/daylight, resting/traveling on, confusion of thought/clarity, sense of menace/of ease, imprisonment or a trap/freedom, fear/courage. ONE OVERSTATEMENT: she writes 'Each such reversal or pulsation occurs more than once in the chapter, some three or four times' — 'three or four times' applies to SOME, not to each. Also she names the chapter 'Fog on the Barrow Downs' (no hyphen).

Both halves confirmed; note she immediately qualifies the up/down rule.

All three components verbatim.

claim: Zimmer argues much of the prose's power comes from a technically skilled poet: Tom Bombadil's dialogue is in amphibrachs and amphimacers, galloping riders get dactylic and wolves spondaic stress patterns.

quote: written by a poet of high technical skill

verdict.trueWording: written by a poet of high technical skill
verdict.note: Wikipedia 'Metrical variety' section: Zimmer quoted as 'much of the power of Tolkien's "prose" comes from the fact that it's written by a poet of high technical skill, who carried his metrical training into his fiction'; Bombadil's whole dialogue in a metre 'built on amphibrachs and amphimacers'. The horses/wolves line is marked by Zimmer as 'dactyl, dactyl, anapaest, anapaest for the galloping riders; the sudden spondee of the wolves' — the claim drops the two anapaests but is otherwise accurate.

claim: Kullmann and Siepmann hold every poem follows a traditional genre and is fitted in style and content to its speaker, and Straubhaar that prose and verse are built to flow as an integrated whole.
source: Wikipedia, 'Poetry in The Lord of the Rings'
quote: fitted in style and contents to the characters

verdict.trueWording: fitted in style and contents to the characters
verdict.note: Quote is on the page word for word — BUT it is Tolkien's own wording from a letter (cited [T 3]), not Kullmann and Siepmann's. Their wording is 'all the poems follow in one traditional genre or another'; the page introduces the letter as corroboration ('Tolkien indeed wrote in a letter that...'). Straubhaar half is confirmed: prose and poetry 'intended and constructed to flow complementarily as an integrated whole.'

claim: Kullmann argues the shift from prose to poetry directs attention from meaning to sound, with hobbit verse in simple iambic tetrameter, Elvish verse in liquid l-sounds, and Rohan's in Old English alliterative metre.
source: Kullmann, 'Poetic Insertions in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings', Connotations 23.2
quote: direct the focus away from meaning to sound

verdict.trueWording: away from the meaning to sound and form
verdict.note: Quote is NOT word for word. Actual: 'The shift from prose to poetry serves to direct the focus of the reader's attention away from the meaning to sound and form, from the signifie to the signifiant.' Other elements supported: iambic tetrameter is 'the most prominent metre found in the novel', used mainly for the walking songs and hymns, and called 'a very simple metre' (though Kullmann does not label it 'hobbit verse'); Elvish l-sounds confirmed ('names that emphasize the letter l ... the elves being -l-ight, -l-iquid, e-l-usive'); Rohan confirmed ('alliterative verse used by the "Ents" and the "Riders of Rohan," which obviously follows the rules of Old English alliterative poetry').

claim: Brauer observes that alliteration crosses from the Rohirrim's verse into the surrounding narrative prose of 'The Ride of the Rohirrim' (e.g. 'Fey he seemed').

verdict.trueWording: makes its way into Tolkien's prose

'Fey he seemed' appears in the quoted prose with the f-alliteration marked.

claim: Thomas, using Booth's scale, finds The Hobbit opens with a very intrusive narrator who recedes as the book darkens, while LOTR's narrator is impartial and self-effacing and early LOTR drafts failed when they tried to return to the intrusive voice.

quote: impartial and self-effacing

verdict.trueWording: impartial and self-effacing

Booth confirmed in the footnote ('a system from Wayne Booth's The Rhetoric of Fiction ... a scale between unintrusive and intrusive'), and the drafts: 'the initial drafts of LotR, which were unsuccessful attempts to return to the intrusive voice'. Every element checks out.

claim: Litschko describes The Hobbit's narrator as an intrusive authorial narrator who comments on and judges characters, addresses readers directly, and carries a patronising quality suited to a young audience.
source: Litschko, 'The Voice of the Narrator in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit' (2006, GRIN preview)
quote: intrusive authorial narrator who frequently comments on and judges

verdict.trueWording: intrusive authorial narrator who frequently comments on and judges
verdict.note: GRIN preview (Litschko, 2006, 29 pp.): 'the narrator of The Hobbit is an intrusive authorial narrator who frequently comments on and judges the characters as well as the unfolding events ... and who addressed his readers in a direct way'. claim: Rateliff records that Tolkien's 1960 rewrite tried to bring The Hobbit into harmony with LOTR's mood, language and geography, and was abandoned because it was losing the humour and no longer read as The Hobbit.
source: Wikipedia, 'The History of The Hobbit' (citing Rateliff, Fisher)
quote: losing much of the humour

verdict.trueWording: just as well that Tolkien abandoned the attempt
verdict.note: Quote 'losing much of the humour' is verbatim, and the harmony motive is on the page (Fisher: the rewrite 'would have refashioned the whole book "to bring it into greater harmony with the mood, language, and geography of The Lord of the Rings"'; Rateliff's stated goal is the 1960 revision 'abortively seeking to harmonize the novel with The Lord of the Rings'). BUT the page nowhere gives a REASON for the abandonment and contains nothing resembling 'no longer read as The Hobbit' — Fisher merely adds 'In his view, it was just as well that Tolkien abandoned the attempt.' The causal clause of the claim is unsupported here.

claim: Kirk (1971), as summarised, treats LOTR as a philological experiment with a deliberate fairy-tale hobbit style, register graded by social standing (Frodo speaks more nobly), and a resistance to Latin-derived vocabulary.
source: rogersdylan blog, 'I Would Rather Have Written in Elvish' (summary of Kirk 1971)
quote: a grand philological experiment

verdict.trueWording: a grand philological experiment
verdict.note: Blog: 'The author of "I Would Rather Have Written in Elvish," Elizabeth D. Kirk, shares the view that Lord of the Rings was a grand philological experiment.' Hobbit style confirmed ('this "Hobbit style" was deliberate and crucial to Tolkien's world creation'; '"Hobbit style" refers to the fairy-tale-esque quality'). TWO CAVEATS: the page gives no date for Kirk (1971 is not stated anywhere on it); and the Frodo register point is the blogger's own view, not Kirk's — prefaced 'It is my opinion that...' ('Frodo's tendency to speak more "nobly" than his Hobbit companions'). The Latinate point appears as the critics' complaint that Tolkien's style 'suffers from his hesitance to use latin-based words', which Kirk defends against.

claim: Bratman distinguishes four styles in the legendarium texts: Annalistic, Antique, Appendical and Philosophical.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's Legendarium: Essays on The History of Middle-earth' (citing Bratman)

claim: Turner's abstract holds The Silmarillion deliberately avoids conventional storytelling features to create a remote textworld that demands reader effort.

OpenAlex returns Turner 2022, 'Style and Intertextual Echoes' (doi 10.1002/9781119691457.ch29), whose abstract reads: "The Silmarillion is felt to be a difficult book that requires a special effort from the reader; the deliberate avoidance of stylistic features associated with storytelling makes the text-world appear remote and difficult to approach." Both halves of the claim (deliberate avoidance; remote text-world demanding reader effort) are supported; the source hyphenates 'text-world'.

claim: Shippey's 'impression of depth' arises from casual mentions of an untold background; Drout, Hitotsubashi and Scavera add that apparent contradictions between accounts give readers the impression of a real and complex history.

The Shippey half is also supported: he is quoted on depth and on "a coherent, consistent, deeply fascinating world about which he had no time [then] to speak", and factor 2 of the four listed factors is "the apparently casual and incomplete mentions of this background in the text".

claim: The Red Book conceit, the Prologue's 'Note on the Shire Records' and the appendices produce an editorial distance mimicking historical recovery; West says the device appeals to the modern mystique of scholarly research.

It functions, he writes, as what scholars would call a spurious source, but the authority it imparts is by an appeal not to the old and familiar, but to the modern mystique of scholarly research." The found-manuscript conceit and the copies/redactions/translations are on the page. claim: Flieger's Interrupted Music presents LOTR as one version of its story embodying references to other versions, with layered narrators, overlapping texts and variants that make the mythology read like a genuine tradition.
source: Wikipedia, 'Interrupted Music'

verdict.trueWording: "multiple narrators, overlapping texts and variant versions"
verdict.note: Both halves verbatim. Flieger's four levels are quoted directly: "as the story itself; as one version of that story embodying references to other versions; as a historical artifact—the Red Book; [and] as a modern edition of that book" (Flieger 2005, p. 80). The quoted phrase is from reviewer Thomas Fornet-Ponse in VII: "Tolkien depicts his work like a true mythology with different layering, multiple narrators, overlapping texts and variant versions" — i.e. a reviewer characterising Flieger's book, which is how the claim uses it.

claim: The interlaced narrative repeatedly leapfrogs between threads, limits the reader to what one Hobbit sees, and uses synchronising narrative landmarks to keep time shifts legible.
source: Wikipedia, 'Interlacing in The Lord of the Rings'
quote: narrative repeatedly leapfrogs

verdict.trueWording: "the narrative repeatedly leapfrogs"
verdict.note: All three elements verbatim. "[T]he books do not end with the characters synchronised; instead, the narrative repeatedly leapfrogs, so that sometimes one group is ahead in time, sometimes another" (West 1975; Shippey 2005). And: "letting the reader know no more than what one Hobbit sees as he struggles forwards" plus "the use of synchronising 'narrative landmarks', such as the brooch dropped by Pippin and discovered by Aragorn" (Holmes 2014).

claim: Agøy's survey of all descriptions in LOTR finds Tolkien's descriptions rarely very detailed, with characters, buildings and scenery described quite vaguely so readers complete the picture.
source: Agøy 2013, 'Vague or Vivid? Descriptions in The Lord of the Rings', Tolkien Studies 10 (abstract via OpenAlex)
quote: Tolkien's descriptions are rarely very detailed

verdict.trueWording: "Tolkien's descriptions are rarely very detailed"
verdict.note: OpenAlex returns Agøy 2013, 'Vague or Vivid?: Descriptions in The Lord of the Rings', Tolkien Studies 10, with the phrase verbatim (typographic apostrophe only difference), followed by "People, buildings and objects are usually described more or less as the scenery or weather is described, quite vaguely, that is; as seen from a distance." The whole-text survey is confirmed: "I have read through the entire main text of The Lord of the Rings slowly and taking detailed notes", and Reid's review in the same result set calls it "a detailed close reading of all descriptions in the novel" whose generality lets "readers fill in the blanks". Note the source says 'objects', not the claim's 'scenery', in that triad.

claim: Walker holds Tolkien's description sounds vividly detailed while actually giving an open-ended outline that lures readers into filling in the blanks.
source: Tolkien Library interview with Steve Walker
quote: lure us into filling in the blanks

verdict.trueWording: "lure us into filling in the blanks"
verdict.note: Verbatim in Walker's own words in the interview: "tolkien's essential stylistic tactic is to lure us into filling in the blanks". The rest of the claim is also verbatim there: "tolkien's writing, too, sounds vividly detailed, as with his descriptions of hobbits, but he's actually giving us an open-ended outline … that invites us to picture for ourselves what Frodo looks like", and he names "[i]ts invitational quality" as the prose's chief appeal.

claim: Lee reports Rateliff's observation that Tolkien often describes a scene not as experienced but as remembered afterwards, and that Walker and Rateliff both call this the 'invitational style'.

quote: as you would remember it afterwards

verdict.trueWording: "as you would remember it afterwards"
verdict.note: Verbatim in Lee's PDF: "Rateliff (2009, 6) suggested that Tolkien 'often describes a scene not as you experience it but as you would remember it afterwards'". The invitational-style attribution is also verbatim, in Lee's footnote 17: "what has been called his 'invitational style' (Walker 2009, and Rateliff 2009)". One nuance the claim flattens: Lee raises the Rateliff observation in order to qualify it for this scene ("but in this instance no single protagonist could have seen all these things"), and the footnote attaches 'invitational style' to non-description of a monster, a different passage from the memory point.

claim: Walker credits the prose with a sense of time that brings past and future into the present; Shippey defends the Lament of the Rohirrim as a paraphrase of The Wanderer's ubi sunt against Manlove's charge of overworked cadences.

verdict.trueWording: Manlove's "overworked cadences" and "monotonous pitch"
verdict.note: The quoted phrase is verbatim on the fetched page: Shippey "replies to Colin Manlove's attack on Tolkien's 'overworked cadences' and 'monotonous pitch' and the suggestion that the Ubi sunt section of the Old English poem The Wanderer is 'real elegy' unlike anything in Tolkien, with the observation that Tolkien's Lament of the Rohirrim is a paraphrase of just that section". The Walker half is NOT on this URL; it is on the companion page the claim's source field also names ('Tolkien's prose style'): "Walker adds that the sense of time which brings the past and the future into the present is created both by Tolkien's ambiguity about the numinous, and by his use of the ubi sunt theme" (Walker 2009, p. 85). Both halves hold, split across the two cited pages.

claim: Reid's Hallidayan analysis of Theme/Subject in three tonally different excerpts finds shared grammar placing the discourses of mythology and history on a continuum that links LOTR to The Silmarillion.
source: Reid 2009, 'Mythology and History: A Stylistic Analysis of The Lord of the Rings', Style 43.4 (abstract via Crossref)
quote: considerably deeper and richer than critics have realized

verdict.trueWording: "considerably deeper and richer than critics have realized"
verdict.note: Crossref returns Reid, 'Mythology and History: A Stylistic Analysis of The Lord of the Rings', Style 43(4), 2009, doi 10.5325/style.43.4.0517. Abstract verbatim for the quote, and for the rest: "drawing on linguist M. A. K. Halliday's functional grammar, focuses on Theme/Subject and the processes in three excerpts from the novel which are different in subject matter, narrative function, and tone. Despite these differences, a stylistic analysis reveals similarities in the text's grammar that show how the discourses of mythology and history in Middle-earth exist on a complex continuum which unobtrusively connects the novel to The Silmarillion."

claim: Chen argues Tolkien's Secondary Belief is produced by a style of hypotyposis (vivid evocation), metalepsis and harmonism across LOTR and The Silmarillion.

Bibliographic details confirm the claim: Fanfan Chen, Caietele Echinox, Issue Year 2014, Issue No. 26, pp. 63-82. The gloss 'vivid evocation' for hypotyposis is the claim's own, not the abstract's.

claim: Livesey's keyness and collocation analysis tracks the Ring from a central to a peripheral place and from a magical to a burdensome device, registering a tonal fall from faerie to darkness across The Hobbit and LOTR.

verdict.trueWording: "the gradual disenchantment of Tolkien's world"

The mechanism is verbatim too: "techniques of keyness and collocation analysis to trace … a) the Ring's transition from a central to a peripheral place in the Third Age's narrative arc; and b) the Ring's progress from a magical to a burdensome device", across "The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings", with the world "falling from a child-like state of mystery, adventure, and faerie, to one of darkness, hierarchy, and amnesia."

claim: Moorcock's 'Epic Pooh' condemns the predominant tone as the prose of the nursery-room, a lullaby meant to soothe and console.

quote: the prose of the nursery-room

verdict.trueWording: "the prose of the nursery-room … a lullaby; it is meant to soothe and console"
verdict.note: Verbatim and correctly attributed: "The fantasy author Michael Moorcock, in his 1978 essay, 'Epic Pooh', compared Tolkien's work to Winnie-the-Pooh. He asserted, citing the third chapter of The Lord of the Rings, that its 'predominant tone' was 'the prose of the nursery-room … a lullaby; it is meant to soothe and console.'" The word 'predominant tone' in the claim is also the page's quoted wording.

claim: Auden's 1954 review credits Tolkien with an amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description.

claim: Lewis's 1955 review praises the romance's very high architectural quality, its two-pattern six-book design, and the fact that no individual or species exists only for the plot.

The page does confirm: the essay 'originally appeared in 1955'; Lewis 'talks about the structure of the work' and admires the parallel books of volumes two and three (discussing books 3 & 5 and 4 & 6, i.e. the six-book design); and verbatim, 'no individual, and no species, seems to exist only for the sake of the plot.' Two of three elements hold; the headline quotation is not on the cited page.

claim: Rateliff calls Tolkien a very careful stylist who weighed the effect of each word, against detractors such as Medcalf, who read sentences aloud to mock them, and Raffel.

quote: deliberately weighed the effect of each word

verdict.trueWording: a v. careful stylist who deliberately weighed the effect of each word
verdict.note: Fully supported. Rateliff writes Tolkien 'is a v. careful stylist who deliberately weighed the effect of each word' (the source abbreviates 'very' as 'v.'; the quoted fragment itself is exact). Detractors confirmed: 'Stephen Medcalf, whom I saw giving a major presentation in which he kept reading out loud individual sentences from LotR and saying how bad they were', and 'Burton Raffel in his essay in Isaacs & Zimbardo... in which he pillories Tolkien's prose'.

claim: Lobdell argues the architecture and narrative style of the Edwardian adventure story (King Solomon's Mines, The Lost World) underlie The Hobbit and LOTR.

The claim's specifics are NOT on this record at all: King Solomon's Mines, The Lost World, and The Hobbit appear nowhere, and the record never says 'architecture and narrative style'. This is an Internet Archive catalog record (blurb + TOC), not the book text, so it can support only the bare Edwardian-influence thesis for LOTR.

claim: Rosebury (as summarised on Wikipedia) shows the Witch-king passage starting in plain syntax and rising into a higher register when it touches ancient and magical history.

verdict.trueWording: begins in plain language, modulating into a higher register
verdict.note: No quotation was supplied, so verbatim status is not assessable; the claim's wording nonetheless tracks the page almost exactly. Lead section: 'He analyses a passage where Merry has just helped to kill the Witch-King. Tolkien begins this in plain language, modulating into a higher register to deal with the echoes of ancient and magical history.' Body confirms Rosebury writes the passage 'begins with "essentially plain syntax"'.

claim: In the same passage Rosebury points to the inversion 'But glad would he have been' and assonance across blade/wield/dealt as deliberate elevation devices.
source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Rosebury 2003)
quote: But glad would he have been

verdict.trueWording: the following 'But glad would he have been', with effective use of inversion
verdict.note: Both devices confirmed in the 'Justified grandeur' section: the inversion is quoted exactly, and the page states the passage 'ends with a powerfully musical sentence with assonances between "blade", "wield", "dealt" and so on', attributed to Rosebury.

claim: Tom Simon argues the narrative opens in a jolly Edwardian style, grows more serious as danger rises, and adopts definite formal archaism in the Rohan chapters.
source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
quote: a jolly Edwardian style

verdict.trueWording: The story begins in a jolly Edwardian style
verdict.note: All three movements confirmed. Opening: 'The story begins in a jolly Edwardian style that hostile reviewers compared to the Boys Own Paper.' Rising seriousness: 'As the road to Rivendell grows more perilous... the narrative style becomes still more serious and uncompromising.' Rohan: 'the Rohan chapters stiffen into definite and formal archaism.'

claim: Simon names Tolkien's mature register 'neo-archaic': archaic in tone and diction while carefully avoiding actual archaic words, with Aragorn the first major character to speak it.
source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
quote: archaic in tone and diction

verdict.trueWording: it is archaic in tone and diction, but he carefully refrains from using archaic words
verdict.note: Exact: 'We might call it Tolkien's neo-archaic style: it is archaic in tone and diction, but he carefully refrains (at this point) from using archaic words. Aragorn is the first major character to employ it in dialogue.' Every element of the claim, including the name 'neo-archaic' and Aragorn's primacy, is on the page.

claim: Once Aragorn enters, Simon says, the narrative's sentence structure itself begins to approximate an older diction rather than relying on antique words.
source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
quote: begins to approximate an older diction

verdict.trueWording: the sentence structure begins to approximate an older diction
verdict.note: Confirmed in context immediately after Aragorn's entrance: 'Once he enters the story, the narrative tone becomes more formal, the prose more cadenced. It is not yet archaic in the strict sense: the words are all familiar to us... But the sentence structure begins to approximate an older diction.' The vocabulary-versus-syntax contrast the claim makes is explicit.

claim: Simon defends archaic inversion by the 'Ask not / Don't ask' test: modernising the word order loses force and rhythm.
source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
quote: loses force and rhythm

verdict.trueWording: Change Ask not to Don't ask, and the sentence loses force and rhythm
verdict.note: Exact, and the framing matches: Simon cites Kennedy's inaugural ('Ask not what your country can do for you') and adds that changing it to 'Do not ask' is 'even worse'. Used to defend the archaism level found through most of LOTR.

claim: Simon argues that putting Théoden's speech about dying honourably into modern idiom would require an insincerity of thought, a disunion of word and meaning.
source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
quote: a disunion of word and meaning

verdict.trueWording: an insincerity of thought, a disunion of word and meaning
verdict.note: Verbatim, and correctly situated: the passage concerns Theoden's 'I myself will go to war, to fall in the front of the battle... Thus shall I sleep better', set against a modernised paraphrase. One attribution nuance worth noting: Simon marks the phrase as Tolkien's own ('It would be, as he calls it, ...'), quoting Tolkien's reply to Hugh Brogan; Simon endorses and elaborates the argument rather than coining the phrase.

claim: Simon reads the Old Forest chapters as sustained phantasmagoria, Bombadil's speech as loose metre, and the Amon Hen scene as a caesura separating the safer from the perilous half of the story.
source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
quote: a kind of caesura

verdict.trueWording: the effect is one of sustained phantasmagoria
verdict.note: All three parts confirmed. 'In the chapters from "The Old Forest" to "Fog on the Barrow-downs", the effect is one of sustained phantasmagoria'; Bombadil 'speaks in verse - a slightly looser version of the rough metre of his signature song'; and Amon Hen 'serves as a kind of caesura, emphatically separating a comparatively safe and comfortable part of the story from the sharply increased perils and higher tone that come after'.

claim: Simon's lesson for fantasy writers is that stylistic choices must serve the story and never call attention to themselves, or they bounce the reader out.
source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
quote: bouncing one out of the story

verdict.trueWording: This is what is meant by the expression 'bouncing one out of the story'
verdict.note: Quotation verbatim, and the lesson is on the page: 'Our grave danger as writers, then, is that we will do something to wrench the reader's attention away from the story and back to the text... we need to keep their minds on the story as much as possible, which generally means keeping it off the text.' One nuance: Simon does not counsel plain invisibility - he explicitly rejects flat prose as 'too flat to engage the emotions' and argues for a broad emotional range, so 'never call attention to themselves' should be read as 'never wrench attention from story to text'.

claim: Reviewing The Children of Húrin, Simon says Tolkien's signature trick is coupling archaic syntax with deliberately ordinary vocabulary.
source: Tom Simon, The Children of Húrin review (Bondwine, 2007-05-19)
quote: coupling archaic syntax with deliberately ordinary vocabulary
page: The Children of Húrin, by J. R. R. Tolkien

verdict.trueWording: coupling archaic syntax with deliberately ordinary vocabulary
verdict.note: Exact, in the 2007 Children of Hurin review: 'Tolkien produced many of his best effects by coupling archaic syntax with deliberately ordinary vocabulary.' Context is his discussion of 'haply' as an unusually archaic word for the book, which he treats as the exception to this signature technique.

claim: Simon relays Tolkien's own defence that real archaic English is terser than modern English, illustrated by 'haply' carrying a whole clause of fatality.

verdict.trueWording: Real archaic English is far more terse than modern

Simon explicitly frames it as Tolkien's own defence: "The best answer is the one he gave to Hugh Brogan". The haply illustration is present too: "That takes twelve words to Tolkien's seven" and "Morwen's almost parenthetical use of haply expresses all the fatality of her decision and the fatalism of her outlook". (My first fixed-width grep falsely reported this absent; the line is short and standalone.)

claim: Simon describes the late Silmarillion prose as a cold and august style that cannot bend to everyday incident, whereas the early Lost Tales were vivid and immediate.

Like Treebeard, it was 'not very, hm, bendable'." The Lost Tales contrast is also verbatim: that style is "quite different: occasionally twee ... but vivid and immediate". Both halves of the claim hold.

claim: Walker (per Wikipedia) finds truly archaic words like alas, thou, whither are rare; the antique feel comes from words such as deem, moot and wight rather than Old English.

Page: "He notes that there are only a few actually archaic words, and that Tolkien uses them only rarely, such as 'alas', 'thou', and 'whither'" and "Walker comments, however, that much of the impression of antiquity comes not from Old English but from more recent, more familiar words such as 'deem', 'moot', and 'wight'". Attributed on-page to Steve Walker, The Power of Tolkien's Prose.

Minor hedge dropped by the claim: the source says "partly due", not simply attributes.

Scope nuance: the obsolescence remark is made specifically of "the keywords used to describe its settings", slightly narrower than the claim's blanket application to all four sets.

claim: Siepmann finds Tolkien prefers the homeliest collocations yet pairs everyday adjectives like 'great' unusually with abstractions, objects and weather, and leans on hyperbole domains (entire/maximum, loud, heavy, tall).

verdict.trueWording: a marked preference for the most homely collocations available
verdict.note: Verbatim. The great pairings match the source's three meaning groups (abstract nouns, concrete objects, natural phenomena including weather), introduced by "Tolkien also uses everyday adjectives in what would have been considered unusual collocations even in his day". One inaccuracy: the hyperbole hypothesis rests on "the last five domains" — speed, entire/maximum, sound:loud, temperature:hot/on fire, long/tall/wide. 'weight: heavy' is listed as a descriptivity source but falls outside those five, so the claim's inclusion of "heavy" among the hyperbole domains is slightly off.

claim: Siepmann concludes Tolkien's prose deploys several centuries of English at once, putting old words to new uses and vice versa, making him a quiet linguistic postmodernist.

verdict.trueWording: he is a linguistic postmodernist

In a much less obvious sense than in the case of James Joyce or Virginia Woolf, he is a linguistic postmodernist." The claim's "quiet" fairly renders "In a much less obvious sense".

claim: Gordon relays Tolkien's point that a king who spoke in modern fashion would not have had those thoughts, so speech register encodes character and culture.

Substance is fully sound, including the 'does not simply mean silver' half: "They think argent 'means' silver. But it does not." Downgraded on contiguity only.

Nothing on this page connects rusticity to a plain modern speech register; that clause is the claimant's own gloss, not Tolkien's. The quoted definition itself is exact.

Adjacent context (moons and sunsets worked out to 1942 almanac) supports the consistency reading, so the gloss is defensible, but it is not the source's wording.

Both halves of the claim are on the page verbatim.

claim: Tolkien condemns colloquialism and false modernity, preferring 'striking' and 'smiting' to 'hitting' and 'whacking'.
source: Wikipedia, 'On Translating Beowulf'
quote: colloquialism and false modernity

verdict.trueWording: colloquialism and false modernity
verdict.note: Wikipedia: Tolkien's insistence that prose Beowulf translations "should be 'harmonious' and should avoid 'colloquialism and false modernity'", and "He advises the translator to prefer 'striking' and 'smiting', and to avoid 'hitting' and 'whacking'." Note the page also records the counterweight: he criticises Morris's "dead and unintelligible 'leeds'", so the preference is not archaism without limit.

claim: Tolkien's rule for heroic diction is to avoid both the colloquial and the obscure, being antiquated without being arcane.
source: Philip Irving Mitchell, 'Tolkien on Translating Beowulf' (DBU)
quote: intentionally antiquated but not intentionally arcane

verdict.trueWording: intentionally antiquated but not intentionally arcane
verdict.note: DBU page (Mitchell): "Tolkien argues that the language of Beowulf for its time was intentionally antiquated but not intentionally arcane; therefore, a good modern translation should avoid both the colloquial and the obscure." Both halves of the claim are on the page. Minor framing caveat: the page states this as advice for translating Beowulf, not as a general rule for 'heroic diction'; it is Mitchell's summary of Tolkien's essay, not Tolkien's own sentence.

claim: Tolkien holds that basic pleasure in the phonetic elements of a language is fundamental and prior to literary enjoyment, citing 'cellar door'.

verdict.trueWording: is of fundamental importance... more immediate than the enjoyment of literature
verdict.note: Wikiquote, under the section 'English and Welsh (1955)': "The basic pleasure in the phonetic elements of a language and in the style of their patterns, and then in a higher dimension, pleasure in the association of these word-forms with meanings, is of fundamental importance... It is simpler, deeper-rooted, and yet more immediate than the enjoyment of literature." The 'prior to literary enjoyment' gloss is supported. 'Cellar door' is supported by the immediately following bullet from the same lecture: "Most English-speaking people... will admit that cellar door is 'beautiful'" — adjacent, not inside the quoted sentence.

claim: Tolkien shows how a pleasing sound like 'cellar door' can become a name and then a character and situation.

verdict.trueWording: and from that a character, a situation begins to grow
verdict.note: Anna Smol quotes a 1966 Tolkien interview (via the Zaleskis' The Fellowship, p. 25): "supposing you say some quite ordinary words to me — 'cellar door,' say. From that, I might think of a name, 'Selador,' and from that a character, a situation begins to grow." The sound-to-name-to-character progression in the claim is exactly the source's.

feature: elegiac annalist tone of The Silmarillion

verdict.trueWording: telling of things already old and weighted with regret

Caveat: the quoted phrase is J.R.R. Tolkien's, about Beowulf, quoted by Christopher and applied by him to The Silmarillion.

claim: Le Guin says Tolkien writes plain clear English whose virtue is flexibility, ranging from commonplace to stately and sliding into verse unnoticed.

verdict.trueWording: It ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately

It ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately, and can slide into metrical poetry, as in the Tom Bombadil episode, without the careless readers even noticing." Every element of the claim, including the unnoticed slide into verse, is present.

claim: Le Guin finds the Council of Elrond dialogue extraordinary for its simple timelessness, with sobriety, wit and force.

It has sobriety, wit, and force." Caveat: Le Guin never names 'the Council of Elrond'; her third passage is footnoted to The Fellowship of the Ring (Ballantine 1965, p. 351) and its speakers are Aragorn, Boromir and Elrond — i.e. the Council of Elrond, an accurate but inferred label.

claim: Le Guin's test is to swap fantasy names for mundane ones; genuine fantasy dialogue survives because speech expresses character, as Boromir's slight whine shows.
source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie'
quote: Speech expresses character.

verdict.trueWording: Speech expresses character.
verdict.note: Le Guin PDF: "Speech expresses character. It does so whether the speaker or the author knows it or not." The name-substitution test is on the page: she rewrites the Kurtz passage "by changing four words" (council lords→committee chairmen, Bran Coris→Brian Corliss, Cardosa→Poughkeepsie, garden→White House garden), then says of the Eddison/Morris/Tolkien passages, "You could not pull the trick on them that I pulled on Morgan and Nigel." Boromir: "the very slight whine in Boromir's tone is significant also."

claim: Le Guin notes Tolkien's vocabulary is not striking and everything is direct, concrete and simple, with none of the fake-archaic 'ichor' register.

verdict.trueWording: he has no ichor; everything is direct, concrete, and simple
verdict.note: Le Guin PDF: "Tolkien's vocabulary is not striking; he has no ichor; everything is direct, concrete, and simple." The claim's 'not striking' and 'direct, concrete and simple' are both the source's own words. 'Ichor' is her term for the fake-archaic register she attacks ("ichor... out of severed tentacles").

claim: Le Guin warns the archaic manner is a perfect distancer only if done perfectly, and faults alternating slang with formal usage as breaking character coherence.
source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie'
quote: It's a high wire: one slip spoils all.

verdict.trueWording: It's a high wire: one slip spoils all.
verdict.note: Le Guin PDF: "The archaic manner is indeed a perfect distancer, but you have to do it perfectly. It's a high wire: one slip spoils all." The second half of the claim is also supported, in a separate passage on Leiber and Zelazny: "they alternate the two styles... colloquial American English, or even slang, and at earnest moments they revert to old formal usages... the characters lose coherence in my mind, and I lose confidence in them."

claim: Le Guin argues that in fantasy style is not an ingredient but the book itself, since every word counts where speech is creation.
source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie'
quote: The style, of course, is the book.

verdict.trueWording: The style, of course, is the book.
verdict.note: Le Guin PDF: "Many readers, many critics, and most editors speak of style as if it were an ingredient of a book, like the sugar in a cake... The style, of course, is the book... This is partly true of history; largely true of fiction; and absolutely true of fantasy." The 'every word counts / speech is creation' rationale is also on the page: "where the act of speech is the act of creation... And every word counts."

claim: Le Guin identifies a two-beat stress/release pulse, like breath or walking gait, as the fundamental rhythm carrying the whole narrative.

quote: Stress, release. Inbreath, outbreath.

verdict.trueWording: Stress, release. Inbreath, outbreath. A heartbeat. A walking gait
verdict.note: Kate Nepveu's post quotes Le Guin's thesis: "the rhythm that shapes and directs his narrative... is very strong and very simple, as simple as a rhythm can be: two beats. Stress, release. Inbreath, outbreath. A heartbeat. A walking gait — but on so vast a scale... that it carries the whole enormous narrative straight through from beginning to end." Breath, gait and whole-narrative carriage are all in the claim and all in the source.

The claim's 'structural rather than incidental' is carried by the source's own word 'fundamental to the structure'.
